sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content: Global equities rebounded from the prior week's AI-driven washout, though gains were uneven across regions. MSCI World rose roughly **1.5%**, with MSCI Developed Markets broadly similar and MSCI Emerging Markets flat to lower as Asian weakness offset the developed-market bounce. In the US the S&P 500 added **2.5%** to **7,561.67** — its best week since August — the Nasdaq Composite gained **2.3%** to **25,136.27** and the Dow rose **2.1%** to **52,347.55**. The mega-cap MAG7 cohort was mixed, with chip peers rallying sharply before Nvidia slid on news of CEO Jensen Huang's resignation. Europe's Euro Stoxx 50 closed near **6,399** as the STOXX 600 logged its best week since June, up about **2.4%**. In APAC the moves diverged: Japan's Nikkei 225 was soft near **61,142**, China's CSI 300 ended little changed near **4,016**, and Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell to around **23,650**, a third straight weekly decline.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equities rebounded sharply from the prior week's AI-led sell-off, posting their first winning week since October. The S&P 500 climbed **2.5%** to **7,561.67**, its biggest weekly gain since August, the Nasdaq Composite rose **2.3%** to **25,136.27** and the Dow added **2.1%** to **52,347.55**. A **2.35%** Monday surge set the tone, and the S&P peaked at **7,619.38** on Wednesday before a softer Friday.

Semiconductors drove the swings. Chip names rallied hard early in the week, with AMD and Broadcom each up roughly **18%**, before Nvidia slid on Friday following the surprise resignation of CEO Jensen Huang, which unsettled AI sentiment. The MAG7 cohort finished mixed as investors weighed leadership risk against still-robust AI demand.

Macro data complicated the recovery. A third consecutive hot CPI print and PPI accelerating to **6.5%** year on year — the fastest since November 2022 — reinforced sticky-inflation fears, while several Fed officials struck a hawkish tone, with some signalling openness to a **50bp** hike. Rising UST yields capped gains into the weekend.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities outperformed, with the STOXX 600 closing at a record **664.14** and logging its best week since June, up about **2.4%**. Strong corporate earnings underpinned the advance, lifting the UK's FTSE 100 to **10,902.56** and leaving Germany's DAX near **26,750**, while the Euro Stoxx 50 held around **6,399**.

Sector dispersion was pronounced. Insurers and oil majors powered the rally and offset a chip-led drag from Nvidia's leadership turmoil, which weighed on semiconductor-exposed names such as ASML. The regional mix left Europe largely insulated from the US tech wobble, a notable divergence from Wall Street's growth-led volatility.

The macro backdrop stayed supportive despite a global bond sell-off. Firmer earnings and relatively contained domestic inflation data helped European shares shrug off rising US yields and dollar strength, though hawkish central-bank commentary abroad tempered enthusiasm and kept the most rate-sensitive sectors in check.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asian markets lagged the developed-market rebound. Japan's Nikkei 225 stayed soft near **61,142**, down roughly **3%** month-to-date, as a firmer yen bias and global tech weakness weighed, even as the BoJ retained a hawkish hold.

Chinese equities were mixed to lower. The CSI 300 ended little changed near **4,016**, pausing after October's heavy falls, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng dropped **1.55%** on Friday to around **23,650**, a third straight session of declines amid fading risk appetite and soft property sentiment.

The semiconductor cycle dominated. Nvidia's CEO resignation and renewed AI-valuation jitters rippled through Asian chip suppliers and exporters, offsetting pockets of policy optimism. Regional sentiment remained hostage to US rate expectations and a stronger dollar, which pressured several EM Asian currencies and equity flows.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar dominated, climbing to one-year highs as sticky US inflation and renewed Fed hawkishness lifted Treasury yields and widened rate differentials. Convera's weekly report framed the move as yield- and risk-driven, with safe-haven demand amplified by geopolitical tensions.

Major currencies struggled against the greenback. EUR/USD slipped toward **1.10**, breaking below its **1.1150–1.1250** range with December's Fed meeting in focus, while GBP/USD fell more than **2%** after testing **1.35** the prior week. The yen drew only limited support from the BoJ's hawkish hold.

Emerging-market currencies came under broad pressure as higher US yields and a firmer dollar sapped carry appeal and spurred outflows, particularly across Asia. Rate-differential dynamics, rather than domestic catalysts, remained the dominant driver of FX price action through the week.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Commodities softened as the stronger dollar and higher real yields dominated. Saxo highlighted gold's technical breakdown, with bullion falling more than **2.5%** to around **$3,881** an ounce and needing to reclaim **$4,000** to improve its outlook; managed-money longs were cut to a five-month low.

Energy extended losses. Crude headed for a second straight weekly decline, with WTI near **$88.90** (down about **2.5%**) and Brent around **$96.40** (off roughly **2.4%**), though prices recovered modestly into Friday as Middle East supply risks kept the physical market on edge.

The cross-asset message was coherent: rising yields and a firmer dollar undercut inflation hedges and rate-sensitive metals, even as lingering geopolitical premia limited the downside in oil. Industrial-demand signals stayed muted, leaving commodities broadly on the back foot through the week.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
Government bonds sold off sharply as hot inflation data and hawkish Fed rhetoric repriced the rate path. The 10-year UST yield jumped roughly **29bp** to about **5.15%**, while the 2-year surged around **35bp**, flattening the curve as markets trimmed expectations for near-term easing.

The catalyst was clear. A third consecutive above-consensus CPI print and PPI at **6.5%** year on year, alongside Fed officials signalling openness to a larger **50bp** move, drove yields toward multi-decade-area highs and lifted the dollar in tandem.

Credit held up relatively well against the rate shock. IG and HY tone stayed broadly firm, supported by the equity-market rebound and resilient earnings, though wider rate volatility and sticky inflation kept risk premia from compressing meaningfully into the weekend.
